questions.q: In which year was the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act passed, and which government enacted it?
questions.a: The 44th Amendment Act was passed in 1978 by the Janata Party government led by Prime Minister Morarji Desai. A wrong answer (e.g., "1976 by Indira Gandhi" or "1980 by Congress") reveals confusion between the 42nd Amendment (Emergency-era) and the 44th Amendment (post-Emergency corrective), and/or misunderstanding of which party was in power when.

questions.q: Explain why the Janata Party government, despite winning a historic mandate in 1977, lost power within two and a half years.
questions.a: The Janata Party collapsed due to: (1) ideological incoherence — it combined socialists, former Congressmen, Hindu nationalists, and liberals with no common programme; (2) leadership rivalry between Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, and Jagjivan Ram; (3) failure to address economic problems (inflation, drought, industrial unrest); (4) perception of vendetta politics (trials of Emergency-era leaders); and (5) dual loyalty of Charan Singh and Raj Narain who split the party. A wrong answer that blames only "Indira Gandhi's popularity" misses the structural weaknesses of the coalition.

questions.q: A student argues: "The 44th Amendment made the right to property a fundamental right again." Identify the error and state the correct position.
questions.a: The error: the 44th Amendment did NOT restore property as a fundamental right. It deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, and inserted Article 300A, making property a constitutional/legal right — enforceable against the executive but not part of the fundamental rights chapter (Part III). A student who says it became a fundamental right again confuses the 44th Amendment with the pre-1978 position (before the 44th, the 42nd had already weakened property rights; the 44th removed them from Part III entirely).

questions.q: Compare the grounds for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352 before the 42nd Amendment, after the 42nd Amendment, and after the 44th Amendment.
questions.a: Pre‑42nd: "war, external aggression, or internal disturbance." 42nd Amendment: replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" but also allowed Emergency to be proclaimed for the whole of India or any part, and made judicial review nearly impossible. 44th Amendment: restored "armed rebellion" as the only internal ground (replacing "internal disturbance"), required written Cabinet advice to the President, mandated parliamentary approval within one month by special majority, and allowed Lok Sabha to disapprove/revoke Emergency by simple majority. A wrong answer that says the 44th Amendment brought back "internal disturbance" shows confusion between the 42nd and 44th changes.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The 1980 election verdict was primarily a rejection of the Janata Party's non‑performance rather than an endorsement of Indira Gandhi's Emergency record." Provide two arguments for and two against.
questions.a: For: (1) Janata's internal feuds and policy paralysis dominated voter discourse; (2) Congress (I) campaigned on "stability" and "strong government," not Emergency achievements. Against: (1) Indira Gandhi's personal popularity surged after her arrest and trial (sympathy vote); (2) Congress (I) won 353 seats — a mandate too large to be only a negative vote. A one‑sided answer ("only Janata's failure" or "only Indira's charisma") fails to weigh both structural and personality factors.

questions.q: Draft a one‑paragraph constitutional provision that could have prevented the misuse of Article 356 (President's Rule) seen in 1977 and 1980, using language similar to the 44th Amendment's safeguards for Article 352.
questions.a: Sample answer: "Article 356 shall not be invoked unless the Governor's report is approved in writing by the Council of Ministers of the State; such proclamation must be laid before each House of Parliament and cease to operate unless approved by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a majority of not less than two‑thirds of members present and voting within thirty days; the Legislative Assembly shall not be dissolved unless the proclamation is so approved." A poor answer copies Article 352 safeguards verbatim without adapting to Article 356's distinct context (state vs. national emergency).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ of the Congress in 1980 refers to the return of Indira Gandhi's Congress (I) to power with a decisive majority in the January 1980 Lok Sabha elections, following the collapse of the Janata Party government (1977–79).

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are reading a 1980 newspaper headline: "Indira Gandhi Returns with a Landslide." Start by asking: why did voters reject the Janata Party that had promised to ______ democracy?

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are reading a ______ newspaper headline: "Indira Gandhi Returns with a Landslide." Start by asking: why did voters reject the Janata Party that had promised to restore democracy?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the political factors that led to the Janata Party's collapse and Congress's return in 1980, and can evaluate the specific provisions of the 44th Amendment that re‑established democratic checks and balances weakened during the Emergency.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are reading a 1980 ______ headline: "Indira Gandhi Returns with a Landslide." Start by asking: why did voters reject the Janata Party that had promised to restore democracy?
